10401-personal-memoir-of-daniel-drayton-:
Daniel Drayton published this memoir in 1855, telling how he spent four years and four months in Washington jail for charity's sake. Drayton, a New Jersey-born sea captain, had tried to carry enslaved people to freedom aboard the schooner Pearl. The voyage and capture form the heart of the book.

Drayton traces his youth on Nantuxet Creek, his life at sea, and the Pearl plan, then prison, trial, and the toll on his health. Profits from the book were pledged to help him, since illness barred hard labor. Readers get a brave, first-hand account of the Underground Railroad at sea and its cost.
11168-life-of-st-declan-of-ardmore-and-l:
Rev. P. Power of University College, Cork, edited this 1914 volume of the Irish Texts Society, giving the Life of St. Declan of Ardmore, from a manuscript in the Royal Library at Brussels, and the Life of St. Mochuda of Lismore, from the Royal Irish Academy, with introduction, translation, and notes. Power values the tracts historically, not philologically, hoping to light up dark corners of the Celtic ecclesiastical past.

Hagiography, Power notes, is the least popularly familiar class of ancient Irish literature, yet as valuable as it is distinctive. In one episode, the pagan host Dercan orders servants to kill a dog, bury its head and feet, cook its flesh, and set it before Declan as mutton. Declan, waking, observes the ministry of the devil in the meat and questions the waiters. The volume makes two early Irish saints' lives accessible to historians.
1278-penelope-s-english-experiences-bein:
Kate Douglas Wiggin sends Penelope, her American traveler, to England, where she tours London, the countryside, and country houses, writing home in letters full of humor and observation. The tale follows Penelope and her friends through tea parties, cathedrals, and comic mishaps.

Wiggin writes England with a tourist's delight and a novelist's eye for manners. The book is light, sunny, and full of local color. It suits readers who liked her Scottish volume and want the English companion to it. Wiggin's English letters match her Scottish volume in sunny humor.
13604-thrilling-stories-of-the-ocean-fro:
Marmaduke Park's 1852 book for young readers gathers sea stories drawn from accounts by modern voyagers and travellers, with many illustrations. It was meant both to entertain and to instruct, and it ranges across sharks, storms, wrecks, battles, and strange creatures of the deep.

One tale follows a sailor who falls among white sharks, while others retell naval fights, including Lord Nelson's signal at Trafalgar, and crews clinging to wrecks for days. The tone is brisk and moral, praising courage and steady conduct at sea. As a boys' book of its day it shows how the ocean was sold to young readers: danger, daring, and hard lessons.
15470-inez-a-tale-of-the-alamo:
Augusta J. Evans, author of Beulah and St. Elmo, published this tale of the Alamo in New York with the Federal Book Company. It is dedicated to the Texan patriots who unfurled the banner of the Lone Star and wrenched asunder the iron bands of despotic Mexico. The dedication sets the book's sympathies before the story starts.

The tale opens not at the Alamo but at a girls' boarding school, where Mary Irving and her cousin Florry rise for prayers, solve problems, and translate Telemachus. Letters, offers of love and fortune, and talk of privation in a new land soon pull Mary toward harder choices. Evans blends schoolgirl romance with Texas history, and the Alamo's shadow falls across a story of faith, love, and loyalty in a young republic.
16928-the-romance-of-a-pro-consul-being-:
James Milne wrote this personal life and memoirs of Sir George Grey, issued by Thomas Nelson in London, Edinburgh, Dublin, and New York. Milne calls Grey the father of federation, who saw that the future of English-speaking peoples rested in a federal idea of communion and government. Grey labored for it in overseas commonwealths, and South Africa, Milne says, had lately answered.

Milne paints Grey as a spacious, high-minded pro-consul, a Walter Raleigh of the Victorians, whose life speaks though he is dead. The book mixes memoir with Milne's own praise of federation. Readers of empire history will find a warm, period life of a colonial statesman, useful for its ideal of federation and its view of Grey's age.
18913-hardy-perennials-and-old-fashioned:
John Wood's guide to hardy perennials and old-fashioned flowers, published by L. Upcott Gill of London in 1884, describes the most desirable plants for borders, rockeries, and shrubberies. Wood writes from plants grown with his own hands in his garden at Kirkstall, for the less experienced amateur.

Perennials, he argues, give variety of form, foliage, and flower with far less trouble than annuals and tender plants, and rightly chosen they bloom more or less through the year. Winter cheer comes from bluet, violet, primrose, Christmas rose, crocus, hepatica, squills, and snowdrops in warm nooks. The book teaches selection by month, so no garden stands forlorn after a single season of bloom.
19356-golden-stories-a-selection-of-the-:
The 1909 volume Golden Stories selects the best fiction by foremost writers. It holds two sections of twelve stories each. Fred M. White opens with The Night Express, a bank robbery tale. Rain pelts a terminus dome and wind booms in the roof. Passengers hurry along. Other stories follow in like popular style.

A detective named Merrick traces eight thousand pounds in gold. He follows the Essex and Norfolk marshes, where a dead man lies in fowling nets at the Little Ouse. No watcher saw aught suspicious. Readers get a rich Edwardian story anthology of crime, adventure, and romance.
20426-form-and-function-a-contribution-t:
E. S. Russell's Form and Function traces how thinkers have explained the shapes of animals. It is a history of animal morphology, the study of how bodies are built. Russell follows ideas from the ancient Greeks to his own day.

The first name in the record, he writes, is Alcmaeon, who lived in the time of Pythagoras. Alcmaeon's interests were more about how the body works than how it is built. He traced the chief nerves of sense to the brain. From such starts, Russell shows how the science of form slowly found its questions.
21056-among-the-great-masters-of-music-s:
Walter Rowlands supplied the text for this 1906 London volume, which pairs scenes from famous musicians' lives with thirty-two reproductions of well-known paintings. It begins with St. Cecilia, the patron saint of music honoured by Christians since early centuries. From her legend it moves through centuries of composers and makers.

Chapters treat Palestrina, Bach, Handel, Gluck, Mozart, Haydn, Beethoven, Schubert, and Paganini, among many others. Violin maker Stradivarius and composer Tartini stand beside singers and keyboard masters. Short, picture-led scenes make the book an easy first tour of music history for general readers of its day.
25531-representative-plays-by-american-d:
Clyde Fitch's play The Moth and the Flame appears here with a long introductory sketch of the playwright, who lived from 1865 to 1909. The editor, who knew Fitch as a friend, recalls his quick talk, his eye for middle-class quirks, and his habit of carrying characters in mind for years before writing.

Fitch brought a literary yet lively style to the American stage, turning out original plays and adaptations from French and German sources with seeming ease. The introduction stresses his good-humoured satire of the social set he knew best, a quality that shapes the play text that follows.
26544-the-dance-festivals-of-the-alaskan:
E. W. Hawkes published this anthropological study in 1914 with the University of Pennsylvania Museum. It describes the ceremonial dances of the Alaskan Eskimo. The text calls the dance a rhythmic pantomime in gesture and song. Dances tell in movement the lives of Arctic animals on which the people lived. The people believed their ancient clans were sprung from those animals.

Hawkes covers the dance house, the kásgi, and the drum chorus of six to ten men. He sets out the steps of men's and women's dances. He then describes the great winter festivals held from November to March. They include the Asking Festival, the Bladder Feast, feasts to the dead, and the great feast. Gifts, trade between tribes, and ritual clothing all play a part in the season.
287-remember-the-alamo:
Amelia E. Barr opens in 1692, when Franciscan monks began a city in a lovely wilderness. Remember the Alamo traces San Antonio from mission days to the famous siege, through mountains, rivers, and singing birds. The city's beauty frames its later bloodshed.

Barr follows settlers, soldiers, and families toward the Alamo's stand, with Wordsworth and Arnold as epigraphs. Her romance mixes history with sentiment in the manner of its age. The novel kept the Alamo legend alive for Victorian readers. It remains a period piece of Texas myth. Barr's Texas romance appealed to readers who loved history with sentiment.
30267-remember-the-alamo:
R. R. Fehrenbach tells a blood-chilling tale of the Alamo in Analog, December 1961, with pictures by Schoenherr. An editorial note calls it one of the most powerful comments on social philosophy the editor had seen. Toward sundown, a man calling himself Ord brings Lieutenant Colonel William Barrett Travis word that Mexican light cavalry have invested Bexar, with light guns set up across the San Antonio River.

Even as Ord speaks, a flash and bang from the west send a shell screaming over the mission walls, and Travis looks worried. Ord is a Britainer or other foreigner, with an odd accent and good Spanish, and seeming knowledge of everything. He reassures him that Santa Anna's guns amount to a few one-pounders, far below respectable siege caliber. In four or five days Ord has become useful to Travis.
4553-st-elmo:
Augusta J. Evans, author of Beulah, Macaria, and At the Mercy of Tiberius, published St. Elmo as a long Southern romance. She dedicates it to J. C. Derby, in grateful memory of many years of faithful friendship, and she sets a Ruskin passage at its head. That passage says a true wife is a servant in her husband's house, but a queen in his heart, and it frames the book's ideas about marriage, duty, and moral influence.

At its centre stand a proud, gifted young woman and the troubled man called St. Elmo, whose learning, pride, and past shadow their courtship. Evans writes at length about reading, faith, work, and the place of women in Southern life. Readers get a sweeping, earnest nineteenth-century romance, famous in its day, for readers who like long novels of character, conviction, and slow-won love.
britannica-1911-aconcio-giacomo:
Giacomo Aconcio (1492-1566) was an Italian thinker called a pioneer of religious toleration. He was born at Trent. He left papal doctrine behind him. His revolt went further than Lutheranism did. After stays in Switzerland and Strassburg, he reached England. Elizabeth had just come to the throne. He had studied law and theology. His paid profession was engineering, though. The English government employed him in that craft. He drained Plumstead marshes. He also reported on the fortifications of Berwick.

Ideas give him his real importance. His Stratagemata Satanae appeared in 1565. It calls the dogmatic creeds the stratagems of Satan. Such creeds, he argued, rent the church apart. Aconcio sought the shared core of all creeds. That core alone was essential doctrine. The rest, he held, was immaterial. Most readers repudiated his low common basis.
britannica-1911-alcamo:
Alcamo, a town of Sicily, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in the province of Trapani, twenty-four miles west-south-west of Palermo, and grew fast, from 37,497 people in 1881 to 51,809 in 1901. Its founding is dated to A.D. 828. A Saracenic chief named Al-Kamuk founded it and raised its castle.

That castle still stands, though considerably altered over the centuries. The emperor Frederick II christianised the town in 1233 and moved its site lower down the hill. Some medieval buildings of interest survive in Alcamo. The country around it is very fertile, the entry adds. Trade in agricultural products from that rich district is considerable, and the farming land, more than any monument, underpins the large population the town had reached by 1901.
britannica-1911-aleandro-girolamo:
Aleandro, Girolamo, an Italian cardinal of 1480 to 1542, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Motta near Venice in February 1480, he studied at Venice and knew Erasmus and Aldus Manutius. Young, he was reputed one of the most learned men of his time. Louis XII invited him to Paris in 1508 as professor of belles lettres, and he served briefly as rector of the university.

Service under the prince bishop of Liege led to Rome, where Leo X kept him and made him librarian of the Vatican in 1519. As papal nuncio he attended Charles V's coronation and the diet of Worms, heading the opposition to Luther and urging extreme measures against the reformer. Luther denounced him, and moderates such as Erasmus disapproved. Captured with Francis I at Pavia in 1525, he was ransomed. Later missions to Germany failed to check the new doctrines. He was made cardinal in 1536.
britannica-1911-barocchio-giacomo:
Giacomo Barocchio, or Barozzi, called da Vignola (1507–1573), was an Italian architect, born at Vignola on 1 October 1507. He worked first at Bologna, Piacenza, Assisi, and Perugia, until Pope Julius III called him to Rome as papal architect. In 1564 he succeeded Michelangelo as architect of St Peter's and built parts of that fabric, besides many works in Rome.

His designs served the Escorial in Spain as well. He wrote an excellent work on the Five Orders of Architecture, printed at Rome in 1563, and another on Practical Perspective in 1583. The 1911 Britannica entry calls him a firm upholder of the classic style. Baroque, he held, was corrupting Italian building. A curiosity follows: the word baroque comes from a Spanish term for an uneven pearl. It does not come from his near-matching name.
britannica-1911-batoni-pompeo-girolamo:
Pompeo Girolamo Batoni (1708–1787), an Italian painter born at Lucca, is the subject of a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. In Italy he was held a great painter of the 1700s. The entry credits him with much of the rescue of Italian art from intense mannerism. That strained, showy style had taken hold in the century before him. That claim for his place in art history opens the account of his work.

Praise in the entry is kept within bounds. Batoni's paintings, it says, are not of the highest order of merit. Yet they are mostly graceful in form, well designed in their parts, and matched in colour with a pleasing harmony. His group of Peace and War is thought his best work. He painted a great many pictures, and was also famed for his portraits.
britannica-1911-bayamo:
Bayamo is an old inland city of Cuba, in Santiago province, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on a plain by the Bayamo river, on the north slope of the Sierra Maestra, in rich farm country. Yet it lies cut off from the sea and from any railway, and its older streets run at all widths and angles, crooked in every direction. Its people numbered 4102 in 1907. Bayamo was the third of the seven cities founded by Diego Velázquez, set up in 1513.

Smuggling made its golden age. Safe inland from pirates, Bayamo drove a thriving secret trade down the Cauto river. By the early 1600s it was the leading town of Cuba. A flood in 1616 choked the Cauto, but the hidden trade ran on for two centuries more. In the war of 1868–1878 Bayamo was a rebel stronghold, and it was nearly destroyed by the two sides.
britannica-1911-bergamo:
Bergamo, the ancient Bergomum, is a city and bishop’s see of Lombardy, Italy, capital of its province at the foot of the Alps. It stands where the Brembo and Serio meet, twenty-six miles from Milan, and counted 46,861 people in the commune in 1901. The city splits in two: the old Città Alta on a hill, walled by Venice, and the newer Città Bassa below, joined by a funicular railway.

Santa Maria Maggiore, a Romanesque church founded in 1137, crowns the upper town, with the Cappella Colleoni beside it holding the tombs of Bartolommeo Colleoni and his daughter. Bergamo was the Orobii tribe’s centre, then a Roman town, then a Lombard duchy capital. Milan held it from 1264 to 1428; Venice kept it until 1797.
britannica-1911-cardan-girolamo:
Girolamo Cardan (1501–1576) was an Italian mathematician and physician. He was also a noted astrologer of his age. This 1911 Britannica entry tells his story. He was born at Pavia on 24 September 1501. He was the illegitimate son of a learned Milanese jurist. He studied at Pavia and then at Padua. At Padua he graduated in medicine. Milan's College of Physicians barred him for his birth.

His first book attacked the fallacies of the medical faculty. A fortunate cure then brought him into notice. A senator's patronage won him admission to the college. In 1539 his Practica Arithmeticae Generalis won him wider fame. He then corresponded with Niccolo Tartaglia on cubic equations. Tartaglia shared his secret solution under a solemn oath. Cardan published it in his great treatise on algebra. The entry follows that famous breach of faith and its fallout.
britannica-1911-carissimi-giacomo:
Giacomo Carissimi (c. 1604–1674) was an Italian composer. He was a master of the Roman school of music. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his work, since his life is obscure. He was born about 1604 in Marino, near Rome. Almost nothing is known of his life, the entry admits. At twenty he became chapel-master at Assisi. In 1628 he took the same post at St Apollinaris in Rome. He held that Roman post until his death in 1674.

Two great achievements are ascribed to Carissimi. He developed the recitative that Monteverde had lately introduced. That advance mattered hugely to dramatic music, the entry says. He also invented the chamber-cantata, in the common account. That form displaced the madrigals then in use. His oratorio Jephthah is his best-known published work. It helped fix the form of the oratorio itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartolommeo-f:
Bartolommeo Fumo was a theologian born at Villon, near Piacenza, who died in 1545. Joining the Dominicans young, he advanced in all church sciences, above all canon law. He distinguished himself as inquisitor at Piacenza. His fame rests on the Summa casuum conscientiae, called the golden bracelet, dedicated to Piacenza's Bishop Catelan.

Its Antwerp edition of 1591 and Lyons edition of 1594 rank most important among many. Canonists prized it as a brief digest of all similar explanations since the thirteenth century. In a few clean-cut sentences it also refutes the errors of probabilism. He also wrote a compendious exposition of Paul's and the Catholic epistles, some poems, and the Philothea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bergamo:
Bergamo, a diocesan entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, covers a Lombard city of 45,000 people, said to be of Etruscan foundation. In the anarchy of eleventh-century Italy it became a commune, joining Lombard leagues against the German emperors. Powerful families, the Turriani, Visconti, and Suardi, then took turns ruling it.

From 1797 to 1859 Bergamo shared every political turn of northern Italy, from French rule to Austrian control and then union with Italy. The entry adds bishops, churches, and schools, with industry noted as a constant strength. It is a compact city history with a church list attached.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-john-:
Blessed John of Fermo, more often called John of La Verna, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Fermo in 1259, he died at La Verna in Tuscany in 1322. Precociously pious, he joined the Canons of St. Peter's at Fermo at ten, then, longing for a stricter life, entered the Friars Minor three years later under James of Fallerone.

The order's head sent him to Mount La Verna, where Francis received the stigmata, John spent many years in solitude, prayer, and contemplation on the holy mountain. The entry presents a friar whose long mountain silence became his fame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bonagratia-of:
Bonagratia of Bergamo, a Franciscan theologian and canonist, stood at the center of the dispute over Christ's poverty. Born Boncortese, he died at Munich in 1343. The fight began at Narbonne in 1321 over whether Christ and the apostles owned property in common or in particular. The Perugia chapter of 1322 chose Bonagratia as its voice before the papal curia at Avignon.

John XXII answered with the bull Ad conditorem canonum, denying that ownership could be split from use. At a public consistory in January 1323, Bonagratia openly opposed the constitution and was jailed for a year. Released, he followed Emperor Louis of Bavaria to Munich in 1330 with Michael of Cesena and William of Occam, dying there still excommunicated and buried in the Barfusser church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-como:
Umberto Benigni's entry covers Como, a diocese and town in Lombardy on Lake Como, the ancient Lacus Larius. Celtic in origin and called Comum, it became a Roman colony in 195 B.C. Rhaetian Gauls destroyed it, and Pompeius Strabo rebuilt it as Novocomum. In the tenth century its bishops were also temporal lords. In the eleventh it became a free commune. Milanese devastated it in 1153 for backing Frederick Barbarossa, who rebuilt it in 1158. The Rusca family then ruled, until Franchin Rusca ceded it to the Visconti in 1355.

Como shared Milan's fortunes thereafter and grew into Italy's silk center. Its cathedral, begun in 1396 and finished only in 1595, gained a cupola and small chapels between 1730 and 1744. In 1528 the town passed under Milan's archbishop. The diocese counted 340,000 people, with 325 parishes, three religious houses of men and twelve of women. Benigni thus joins a lakeside town's civic turns to its church life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eskimo:
The Eskimo occupy America's Arctic coast from below Cook Inlet to the Saint Lawrence, over five thousand miles. This includes Labrador, Baffin Land, Ellesmere Land, Greenland's west and south-east coasts, Hudson Bay's northern shores, and the Aleutian Islands. One body, the Yuit, has crossed Bering Strait to Siberia's extreme point. Evidence shows they formerly extended farther south along Hudson Bay and the Saint Lawrence, and perhaps into New England.

Except the Aleut, who differ considerably, the scattered bands are practically homogeneous in language and ethnology. In physique they are of medium stature, strong and hardy, with yellow-brown skin and Mongolian rather than Indian features, though of American origin. In character they are generally peaceable, cheerful, and honest. The Aleut speak a distinct language in two dialects, while the others speak practically one language in several dialects.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fermo:
Fermo is an Italian archdiocese in the province of Ascoli Piceno. A Roman colony of 6,000 men from 264 BC, its great antiquity shows in massive cyclopean walls. With the Pentapolis it passed to the Holy See in the eighth century. Its bishops became counts, then princes ruling the city.

Hohenstaufen sieges, captures, and papal wars shook Fermo again and again across the troubled centuries. A university rose there under Pope Boniface VIII. The celebrated poet Annibale Caro was born in the city of Fermo. The archdiocese counted 117 parishes, 368 secular priests, and some 18,000 souls in 1908.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-haymo:
Ninth-century Benedictine Haymo, Bishop of Halberstadt, was a scholar formed at Fulda beside Rabanus Maurus and at Tours under Alcuin. Returning to Fulda, he served as monastery chancellor, perhaps teaching theology. After a short stay at Hersfeld he was named bishop in the last weeks of 840, dying on 26 March 853.

Rabanus sent him De Universo, twenty-two books of episcopal advice. Haymo followed it: he kept clear of King Louis the German's court, preached often, lived for his diocese, and attended only the Council of Mainz in 847. His genuine works are chiefly Scripture commentaries, in the moral and mystical sense of his age, with an epitome of Eusebius, many sermons, and a treatise on love of the heavenly homeland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacobus-de-te:
Jacobus de Teramo, canonist and bishop from the Palladini family, was born at Teramo in 1349 and died in Poland in 1417. After reading law at Padua, he took up the archdeaconry at Aversa in 1384, and later worked in Rome as secretary of papal briefs and of the Penitentiaria. His bishoprics came in quick order: Monopoli in 1391, Tarentum in 1400, Florence in 1401, and Spoleto in 1410.

While bishop of Spoleto he also ruled the Duchy of Spoleto, and in 1417 Pope Martin V dispatched him as legate to Poland, where he died that same year. Among his writings are a commentary on Lombard's Book of Sentences, printed at Augsburg in 1472, and a dialogue on the Roman pontiff's monarchy. His oddest work, Consolatio peccatorum, sets out a lawsuit between the Devil and Christ.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-majordomo:
Majordomo, from the Latin major domus, was the chief steward of the pope's household. He ranked among the palatine prelates. He also stood among the four prelates di fiocchetto. They took that name because they might deck their horses' harness with violet and peacock-coloured feathers.

His office took clear shape only after Martin V returned from Avignon in 1418. A head steward had existed far earlier. By the sixteenth century a maestro di casa ran the whole household. Under Urban VIII he first bore the title Maggiordomo Pontificio. He formed each new pope's household and judged its officials in civil and criminal cases. After 1870 the prefecture split from the post. The majordomo kept the governorship of the conclave, a seat in the Palatine Commission, direction of the Sistine Chapel, and charge of papal court functions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-of-o:
Nicholas of Osimo, or Auximanus, was a celebrated preacher and author, born at Osimo, Italy, late in the fourteenth century and dead at Rome in 1453. After studying law and earning his Bologna doctorate, he joined the Observant Friars Minor at San Paolo convent. Conspicuous for zeal, learning and preaching, as companion of Saint James of the Marches in Bosnia and Vicar-Provincial of Apulia in 1439, he advanced the Observants.

For them in 1440 he won complete independence from the Conventuals, a privilege soon revoked at Bernardine's desire. He was also Visitator and later Superior of the Holy Land, though many difficulties hindered those offices. Nicholas wrote in Latin and Italian on moral theology, the spiritual life, and Saint Francis's Rule. His works include the Supplementum Summae Pisanellae, a revised and enlarged Summa completed at Milan in 1444 with many early editions. The Italian Quadriga Spirituale covers four principal means of spiritual progress.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-osimo:
Osimo is a diocese in the province of Ascoli Piceno in Italy, set in the lands of the Donation of Pepin. In the wars of popes and Swabian emperors it stood Ghibelline, yet stayed loyal in 1375 when Florentine prompting drove nearly every city of the Papal States to rebel. Later rulers included Pandolfo Malatesta, Francesco Sforza, and Buccolino, who yielded the city to the Holy See in 1494.

Roman walls and baths still survive, and the eighth-century cathedral was restored and enlarged by Bishop Gentilis in 1205. Saints Florentius, Sisinnius, and Diocletius died as martyrs here, and the city honours Saint Leopardus as its first bishop, though the first of certain date is Fortunatus in 649. Gregory IX moved the see to Recanati in 1240 as punishment, and Urban IV restored it after Bishop Rinaldo's plea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palermo:
Palermo is an archdiocese in Sicily, its city built on a Mediterranean inlet, ringed to the south by hills and mountains. Catalfano rises to the east, Monte Pellegrino to the west. Chief among its churches stands the Duomo, built in 1170 by Archbishop Gualtiero Offamiglio on an old basilica turned mosque under Saracen rule.

Its walls bear twelfth- and thirteenth-century frescoes and mosaics, and its first right chapel holds six tombs of Sicilian kings and queens. Gagini sculptures, a Velasquez Assumption, and a crypt with twenty-one archbishops' tombs enrich the cathedral further. San Domenico, from 1300, is the city's largest and loveliest church, and the entry tours Palermo's shrines, convents, and archbishops through later centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-of-berg:
Peter of Bergamo, called Almadura, was a Dominican theologian who died at Piacenza in 1482. He joined the order in his home town, took his degree at Bologna, and served in the Dominican house of studies as master of students and bachelor. The people of Piacenza honoured him as a saint, and Leander Alberti reports miracles through his intercession. His body rests in a crypt beneath the high altar of St. Thomas's chapel.

Every surviving work of his serves St. Thomas Aquinas. His universal index to all Aquinas's works appeared at Bologna in 1475, and his concordance of apparently clashing passages at Basle in 1478. Combined at Venice in 1497, they entered the Roman edition ordered by Pius V as the Tabula aurea, the Golden Table, reprinted as volume twenty-five of the Parma Aquinas in 1873.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-francis-de:
Francis de Geronimo, Jesuit missioner of Naples, spent forty years preaching in towns and villages across the south. Born at Grottaglie on 17 December 1642, he studied humanities and philosophy at Taranto's Jesuit college, then theology and canon law at Naples' Gesu Vecchio. Ordained on 18 March 1666, he spent four years over the college of nobles' pupils, surnamed the holy prefect, before entering the Jesuit novitiate in 1670. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death to 11 May 1716.

After a first year's probation he learned preaching beside an experienced missioner near Otranto. Four more years of town and village missions revealed a wonderful gift for the work, and superiors kept him at it. The entry's early chapters show formation: Taranto schoolboy, Naples student, prefect of nobles, then missioner whose voice became his life's instrument.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-teramo:
Teramo is a diocese in southern Italy, often injured by earthquakes. It stands where the Tordino and Vessola meet, in a fertile district once famed for delf, with ore nearby. Its cathedral mixes styles, its façade like a fortress wall with a Gothic gate, yet holds Bishop Nicola Arcioni's tomb of 1317. S. Domenico and S. Francesco are worth visiting. Ancient Interamnia was seat of the Praecutii, and a Roman colony settled there in 315 BC.

From Interamnia comes the name Abruzzi, adopted by the sixth century. Ruins include an amphitheatre, theatre, and aqueduct. After the Longobard invasion it housed a gastaldo under Spoleto's duke, and Normans annexed it. In 1155 Count Loretello rebelled against King Roger and destroyed the city, rebuilt through Bishop Guido, whose successors won the principality. Bishops of Teramo then pontificated armed, with arms on the altar. The see, subject to Rome, holds 121 parishes and 233 priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Palermo's university grew from the Convent of St Dominic, which may count as its nucleus. There theology and philosophy were taught not only for Dominicans but for the public. In 1469 Father Tommaso Schifaldo lectured there on Latin literature. Father Salvo Cassetta, a theological lecturer with so large a following that he preached in the public square, was also skilled in mathematics.

In 1553 the commune sought a medical school and called the famed Gianfilippo Ingrassia, whose lectures also took place at St Dominic's. In 1555 the commune engaged Dominican professors of philosophy, including the historian Fazello, and the chair of jurisprudence followed in 1556 under Geo. Ant. de Contovo. The entry traces the slow gathering of chairs and faculties into a university, a civic project built on a friary's classrooms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venturino-of-:
Venturino of Bergamo was a Dominican preacher whose fame nearly ruined him. Born in 1304, he took the Friars Preachers' habit at Bergamo in 1319 and won renown preaching across northern Italy from 1328 to 1335. In February 1335 he planned a penitential pilgrimage to Rome with some thirty thousand converts.

Pope Benedict XII, then at Avignon, misunderstood the gathering, suspecting Venturino aimed at the papacy itself, and ordered it stopped. The papal letters missed him, so he reached Rome in March, preached in its churches, and left twelve days later as the pilgrimage dissolved in disorder. Summoned to Avignon, he was imprisoned from 1335 to 1343, restored by Clement VI, and sent to preach a crusade against the Turks, dying at Smyrna in 1346.

doe-osti-3412262-growth-in-heterogeneous: Living tissue heals and adapts — synthetic materials mostly don't. golden-stories-a-selection-of-the-best-f:
The Short Story Company of New York issued Golden Stories in 1909, calling it a selection of the best fiction by the foremost writers. The book is bound in two sections, each with stories numbered one to twelve. A note says each author's name once carried an all-rights-reserved line, since removed. The first tale is The Night Express, and its pages show the kind of goods on offer.

A guard rides a night train with plain deal boxes worth a fortune, a coffin in the next carriage, and a gale outside. He weighs what Poe or Gaboriau would make of a robbery, even as risk closes in. Tales of crime, love, and surprise fill the rest. Such collections brought magazine fiction home to the parlor table, and they show what editors of 1909 thought the best short story could do.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SchweitzerSolom: nsia-SchweitzerSolomon Schweitzer Solomon: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TranscriptsMemo: A letter dated February 15, 1970, discusses reading the transcripts of eight witnesses from Clinton, Louisiana. Those witnesses figured in Jim Garrison's New Orleans investigation of the Kennedy assassination. The writer reports on working through their testimony on paper. The letter shows researchers trading transcripts and notes as they tried to test what the Clinton witnesses had actually said under oath.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia-intelligence: A cable obtained by the National Security Archive through the Freedom of Information Act shows prosecutors at Guantanamo Bay misleading defense lawyers, according to the Archive's account of it. A briefing book page carries that finding under a headline naming both the cable and the misconduct it allegedly documents. The military commissions have fought for two decades over what the defense may know, and a prosecutor's deception strikes at the trials' basic fairness. Only the page capture survives here, marking the Archive's claim and the document behind it.
hardy-perennials-and-old-fashioned-flowe:
John Wood, a gardener of Kirkstall, published Hardy Perennials and Old-Fashioned Flowers at London in 1884, with a picture of a corner of his own garden. His preface notes a growing desire to patronize perennial plants, above all the beautiful varieties known as old-fashioned flowers. They deserve it, he says, for their variety of form, foliage, and flower, and because they cost less care than annuals and tender plants.

The book describes the most desirable plants for borders, rockeries, and shrubberies, foliage plants included. Each gets its character, season, and treatment in plain working terms. Wood writes from his own beds, not from books. The volume is a founding text of the herbaceous revival that William Robinson and Gertrude Jekyll would make famous, and its counsel is still sound for any border.
inez-a-tale-of-the-alamo:
Augusta J. Evans dedicated Inez, a tale of the Alamo, to the Texan patriots of the Lone Star banner. Cousins Mary Irving and Florry meet at a boarding school in the opening chapter. Florry has solved two problems and translated Telemachus before prayers. Mary wishes she shared that love of study and hard subjects.

Mary's cheek pales and her step weakens as weeks pass in a later strand. She stands at a window at sunset, arms stretched toward the sky. Love, faith, and Texas war carry the cousins south. Evans mixes schoolgirl devotion with the Alamo's fame in a popular romance.
life-of-st-declan-of-ardmore-and-life-of:
The Reverend P. Power edited these two Irish saints' lives in 1914. The Irish Texts Society issued the volume as its sixteenth. Declan's life comes from a manuscript in Brussels's royal library. Mochuda's life rests on a Royal Irish Academy manuscript.

Power supplies introduction, translation, and notes for both texts. He values the lives chiefly as historical material, he confesses. They light up dark corners of Ireland's Celtic church past. Power hopes better equipped explorers will follow his blazed track. The Brussels manuscript preserves Declan's life for Power's edition. Carthach, called Mochuda, joined the volume at the secretary's suggestion.
nasa-tm-19630003077-effects-of-gross-loa:
Walter J. Kapryan of Langley wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-71, in January 1960. It studies how a fast mine-laying seaplane behaves on the water. Three changes to the bow shape were tried in the tests. Total weight, called gross load, was varied as well.

Kapryan's summary says the work ran in Langley tank number one. Two bow changes stretched the forebody by ten feet. One stretched it by twenty feet. The team checked how steady the hull ran along its length. Seaplanes must take off and land on water without porpoising or spray damage. Tank data like this shaped hulls before costly flight tests.
nasa-tm-19630004017-an-experimental-inve:
Gary H. Bowman and Raymond C. Savin of Ames wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-114, in December 1959. It tests nylon as a heat shield material for ballistic missiles. The tests ran in an atmosphere entry simulator, a lab that mimics reentry heat. Nylon would char and burn away, carrying heat with it.

Such sacrificial shields are called ablative materials. The team put nylon samples through entry-like heat and flow. They watched how the material melted, charred, and wore down. Missile nose cones face brief, brutal heating on return. A cheap, light shield like nylon could save weight and cost. This early work helped map the choices for missile protection.
nasa-tm-19660028120-the-instrument-funct:
William D. Johnston III wrote this July 1966 report at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland. His subject is a light-measuring instrument called a wide-angle Michelson interferometer spectrometer. In this design, one part moves along a diagonal path. Johnston asks how that motion shapes the instrument's readings.

Every spectrometer blurs the light it measures in its own way. That blur pattern is called the instrument function. Johnston works out the instrument function for this diagonal-motion design. Knowing the blur lets scientists correct their spectra and recover what the light really looked like before the instrument smeared it.
penelope-s-english-experiences-being-ext: The hosted sample shows only the front matter of Penelope's English Experiences, the title page, dedication, and contents, plus the first heading of chapter one. The contents divide her stay into town and country parts, with chapters on a Hyde Park Sunday, a ducal tea-party, tuppenny travels in London, and Comfort Cottage.
personal-memoir-of-daniel-drayton-for-fo:
Daniel Drayton's Personal Memoir tells how he spent four years and four months a prisoner, as the title says, for charity's sake, in Washington jail. The book includes his narrative of the voyage and capture of the schooner Pearl. An advertisement notes that sale profits support Drayton, whose health in prison left him unfit for laborious work.

The Pearl was the vessel that carried dozens of enslaved people out of Washington in a famous escape attempt, and Drayton was her captain. The memoir begins with his birth in New Jersey in 1802 and builds his own defence of the act that ruined him.
podcast-dannyjones-HxsIZ4vVImo:
Geologist Stefan Burns studies the sun's cycles and their effects on the earth. He joins Danny Jones to present a grand pattern. It is a solar cycle of roughly 12,000 years that he says resets civilizations, ending ages in catastrophe and beginning them again.

Burns connects sunspot records, magnetic shifts, and ancient disaster myths into one timetable. Jones asks what the cycle predicts for the present century, which is where the theory earns its audience. Mainstream geology accepts pieces of his physics and rejects the grand cycle built on them. The episode gives the full construction anyway, in the calm voice of a working scientist rather than a prophet. Listeners get a testable-sounding claim about humanity's past and future, and the burden of deciding how much of it the evidence carries.
podcast-joerogan-zZee_5h55mo:
Philosopher Ben Burgis joins Joe Rogan for episode 1783 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Burgis is a professor and writer from the left, known for sharp debate and for a book that roasts cancel culture from his own side. His visit sets up a true clash.

Burgis and Rogan spar over free speech, class, and who the left should fight for. They grant each other room, then strike when a point runs weak. The talk is long and civil, a rare thing for such a split. Listeners who love a real debate get one here. The library keeps the episode as a record of the clash.
remember-the-alamo:
Amelia E. Barr opens this historical novel in a city founded in the wilderness, under Wordsworth and Matthew Arnold verses. Chapter one goes back to 1692, when a few Franciscan monks began to build hundreds of miles from settled life. The site, Barr writes, was as beautiful as the garden of God.

One river, fed by a hundred springs, the monks called the San Antonio, and on its banks they raised three missions. White stone domes, carving, and bright color adorned them, and their bells called to peoples who resisted the newcomers fiercely. Priest, fort, and soldier together made the mission a city wrapped in romance, the ground of the Alamo story.
st-elmo:
Augusta J. Evans, author of Beulah, Macaria, and At the Mercy of Tiberius, wrote St. Elmo. A long quote from John Ruskin heads the book, on a true wife as servant in her husband's house and queen in his heart. Evans gives the pages to J. C. Derby, in fond thanks for many years of kind and faithful friendship. The same Ruskin lines stand again at the head of the tale itself.

Chapter I opens with a child's voice singing the words of the prophet on Shigionoth: He stood and measured the earth, and the everlasting mountains were scattered. The sweet, glad, childish voice sings to a strange, wild tune, solemn as the Hebrew chant of Deborah and as full of triumph. That bright opening, set against the grave Ruskin motto on wives and husbands, frames the book's clash of pure youth and hard duty.
the-romance-of-a-pro-consul-being-the-pe:
James Milne presents Sir George Grey as a father of federation in a people's edition introduced at London in March 1911. Grey died twelve years earlier leaving, Milne says, a message that the future of English-speaking peoples rests on a federal idea of communion and government.

As pro-consul Grey labored for that idea across overseas commonwealths, with South Africa lately answering, while talk of federal home rule marks a turning in British institutions. Milne calls him a Walter Raleigh of the Victorians who still speaks though dead. Biography here doubles as political argument for federation.
thrilling-stories-of-the-ocean-from-auth:
Marmaduke Park compiled Thrilling Stories of the Ocean from authentic accounts of modern voyagers, designed for young people's entertainment and instruction. C. G. Henderson published it at Philadelphia in 1852, with numerous illustrations. An opening piece under the name Volney Beckner turns at once to sharks.

White sharks, Park warns, are the dread of sailors in hot climates, following ships for hundreds of leagues hoping for scraps. A man overboard near one is in grave danger. Some sharks weigh thousands of pounds, and their rough skin polishes wood and ivory. Readers get sea instruction mixed with peril.
